nameStory: Annual Honesty gets its intriguing name from its translucent, papery seed pods that are so thin you can see right through them - as if the plant is being completely 'honest' about what's inside! These silvery, moon-like discs have also earned it the nickname 'money plant' because they resemble shimmering coins hanging from the branches.
description: Annual Honesty is a charming garden escapee that stands 2-4 feet tall with heart-shaped, toothed leaves and clusters of four-petaled purple or white flowers in spring. After blooming, it produces its most distinctive feature: large, flat, circular seed pods that start green but dry to become translucent, silvery discs about the size of a quarter. This member of the mustard family is originally from southern Europe but has naturalized in many New England gardens and nearby wild areas.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Large, flat, circular seed pods that dry to papery, translucent silvery discs - you can hold them up to the light and see right through them like natural windows

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Four-petaled flowers in loose clusters, typically purple, pink, or white, with a sweet, mild fragrance reminiscent of other mustard family plants

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped leaves with pointed tips and coarsely toothed edges, feeling slightly rough and hairy when you run your fingers across them

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright branching plant growing 2-4 feet tall, often forming small colonies in favorable spots with a somewhat open, airy appearance

habitat: Look for Annual Honesty in semi-shaded areas near old gardens, along woodland edges, and in disturbed soils where it has escaped cultivation. It thrives in rich, moist but well-drained soil and often appears in the transition zones between cultivated and wild areas. You'll commonly find it around old homesteads, abandoned gardens, and along paths where seeds have been dispersed.

seasonality.spring: Purple, pink, or white four-petaled flowers bloom in clusters from April to June, filling the air with a sweet, subtle fragrance.
seasonality.summer: Green seed pods develop and gradually mature, while the plant focuses energy on seed production as flowers fade.
seasonality.fall: The most spectacular season - seed pods turn into silvery, translucent discs that catch and reflect autumn light beautifully.
seasonality.winter: Dried stems may persist with papery seed pod remnants, though most above-ground parts die back since this is an annual plant.

funFact: The translucent seed pods are so durable and beautiful that they've been used in flower arrangements for centuries - Victorian ladies would collect them to create 'everlasting bouquets' that could last for years without any water, earning the plant yet another name: 'Satin Flower.'
confusionNotes: The heart-shaped leaves might remind you of violets, but Annual Honesty's four-petaled flowers and upright growth habit quickly set it apart. Those unmistakable silvery seed pods make mature plants impossible to confuse with anything else in New England.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name 'Annual' fool you completely - while individual plants live only one year, Annual Honesty readily self-seeds and can appear perennial in favorable locations. It's also worth noting that despite being in the mustard family, it looks quite different from the typical yellow mustard flowers most people know.
compareHints: Annual Honesty is the only Lunaria species commonly found in New England. Among other mustard family members, it's unique for its large size, heart-shaped leaves, and especially those distinctive large, round, translucent seed pods - most other mustards have much smaller, elongated seed pods. The combination of purple flowers and eventual papery 'coins' makes it unmistakable among its mustard family cousins.
